concepts.text: What a Computer Network Is

A computer network is a set of autonomous devices (nodes) interconnected by communication links so that they can exchange data and share resources such as files, printers and Internet access. A data communication system has five components: message, sender, receiver, transmission medium and protocol. A good network is judged on performance (throughput and delay), reliability (failure frequency and recovery time) and security (protection from unauthorised access and damage). Links may be point-to-point (a dedicated link between two devices) or multipoint (several devices share one link).

concepts.text: Networks are classified by geographic span:
items: PAN (personal area network): a few metres around one person, e.g. Bluetooth between phone and earbuds.
LAN (local area network): a single building or campus, privately owned, high speed (100 Mbps to 10 Gbps Ethernet or Wi-Fi) and low error rate.
MAN (metropolitan area network): covers a city, e.g. a cable TV network or a city-wide fibre ring linking many LANs.
WAN (wide area network): spans a country or continent using leased lines, MPLS, satellite or the Internet; usually owned by carriers and slower per link with higher delay.
Internetwork (internet): two or more networks connected by routers; the Internet is the global public internetwork.

concepts.text: In the client-server model, dedicated servers provide services (web, mail, file, database) and clients request them; administration, security and backup are centralised, but the server can become a bottleneck or single point of failure. In the peer-to-peer (P2P) model every node can act as both client and server and shares its resources directly, as in BitTorrent or a small workgroup; it is cheap and scales with the number of peers but is harder to secure and manage. Many real systems are hybrids, for example a P2P application that uses a central index server.
Protocols and Standards
A protocol is a set of rules that governs data communication; its three key elements are:
items: Syntax: the structure or format of the data, i.e. the order and size of fields (e.g. first 8 bits = source address).
Semantics: the meaning of each field and the action to take on it (e.g. what a given control code means).
Timing: when data should be sent and how fast, so a fast sender does not overwhelm a slow receiver.

concepts.text: Standards guarantee interoperability between equipment from different vendors. De facto standards arise by wide adoption, while de jure standards are formally legislated by recognised bodies. Key bodies are ISO (International Organization for Standardization, author of the OSI model), IEEE (LAN/MAN standards such as 802.3 Ethernet and 802.11 Wi-Fi), ITU-T (telecommunication standards, e.g. X.25, V-series modems), ANSI and EIA/TIA (cabling standards such as Cat5e/Cat6), and IETF, which publishes Internet protocols as RFCs (Requests for Comments), e.g. RFC 791 for IPv4.

concepts.text: In a layered architecture each layer offers services to the layer above through an interface and communicates logically with its peer layer on the other machine using that layer's protocol, which hides complexity and lets one layer change without affecting others. On sending, each layer adds its own header (the data link layer also adds a trailer) to the data from above; this is encapsulation, and the receiver strips headers in reverse order (decapsulation). The OSI model (ISO, 1984) is a reference model with seven layers; it is used for teaching and design, while TCP/IP is the protocol suite actually deployed on the Internet.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Layer Functions, Encapsulation and Protocol Placement
Top-down memory aid 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' (layer 7 to layer 1), with each layer's job in one line:
items: Application (7), where the user interacts: browsers and mail clients use protocols such as HTTP, FTP, SMTP and DNS.

Presentation (6), data formatting: translation between representations (ASCII/Unicode, JPEG, MPEG), compression and encryption. Older notes list SSL here; SSL is obsolete and today's equivalent is TLS 1.2/1.3.
Session (5), manages conversations: opens, maintains and closes dialogues and inserts checkpoints so that a long transfer can resume after a failure.
Transport (4), delivery between processes: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery with flow and error control; UDP is connectionless with low overhead and no retransmission.
Network (3), routing: logical (IP) addressing and choice of path across many networks; IP is the protocol, helped by ICMP and the routing protocols.
Data link (2), frame creation: groups bits into frames, adds MAC addresses and an error-detecting trailer (FCS); examples are Ethernet (802.3) and Wi-Fi (802.11).
Physical (1), raw bits: cables, connectors, voltages, light pulses and radio signals; hubs and repeaters work at this layer.

concepts.text: The TCP/IP model can be remembered as A-T-I-N from the top: Application (OSI 5 to 7), Transport (OSI 4), Internet (OSI 3) and Network Access (OSI 1 and 2). OSI is a reference model used for learning and design, while TCP/IP is the suite that actually runs the Internet. The two were built in opposite orders: the OSI layers were defined first and protocols were written for them later, so the model is general but its protocols never caught on. TCP/IP's protocols came first and the model was drawn afterwards to describe them, so it fits TCP/IP closely but describes other stacks poorly.

concepts.text: Data flow (transmission mode) between two devices takes one of three forms:
items: Simplex: one direction only, like a keyboard sending to a computer or a broadcast transmitter; one side always sends and the other always receives.
Half-duplex: both directions but not at the same time, like a walkie-talkie; whichever side is sending uses the whole channel. Hub-based Ethernet runs half-duplex.
Full-duplex: both directions at the same time, like a telephone call; the capacity is shared between the two directions or separate paths are used. Switched Ethernet links run full-duplex.

concepts.text: How the main standards bodies work:
items: IETF: a proposal starts as an Internet-Draft, which expires after six months unless revised; an approved specification is published as an RFC and matures from Proposed Standard to Internet Standard (RFC 6410 cut the old three levels to two). Not every RFC is a standard: many are informational or experimental.
IEEE 802 committee: 802.1 bridging and VLANs (802.1D, 802.1Q), 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 wireless LAN, 802.15 wireless PAN (802.15.1 was based on Bluetooth, 802.15.4 underlies Zigbee) and 802.16 WiMAX.
ITU-T (formerly CCITT): telephone and WAN standards such as X.25, the V-series modem standards and the G-series transmission standards.
ISO: international standards in every industry, including the OSI reference model; ANSI is the United States member body of ISO, and EIA/TIA write cabling standards.
De facto standards arise from widespread use (HTTP began this way with the first Web browsers), while de jure standards are formally adopted by a recognised body.

concepts.text: Every header carries a field that tells the receiver which protocol above should get the payload, so decapsulation is a chain of lookups. In an Ethernet frame the EtherType is 0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6 or 0x0806 for ARP; in the IPv4 header the Protocol field is 1 for ICMP, 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP; and the destination port finally selects the application process, for example 53 for DNS. A router decapsulates only up to layer 3 and builds a new layer-2 frame for the next hop, so MAC addresses change hop by hop while the source and destination IP addresses stay the same unless NAT rewrites them.

Worked example 1: encapsulating 1,000 bytes of HTTP data (no IP/TCP options)
Application data                      : 1000 bytes
+ TCP header 20        -> segment      = 1020 bytes
+ IPv4 header 20       -> packet       = 1040 bytes
+ Ethernet header 14 + FCS 4 -> frame  = 1058 bytes (dest MAC .. FCS)
+ preamble and SFD 8   -> on the wire  = 1066 bytes
+ inter-frame gap 12   -> link time    = 1078 byte times
Share of link time carrying application data = 1000 / 1078 = 92.8 %

concepts.plainText: Header fraction f = nh / (M + nh) and efficiency = M / (M + nh), for an M-byte message passing n layers that each add an h-byte header

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: header overhead in an n-layer stack
Message M = 400 bytes, n = 5 layers, each adds h = 20 bytes
Headers    = n x h = 5 x 20       = 100 bytes
Sent       = M + nh = 400 + 100   = 500 bytes
Header fraction = 100 / 500       = 20 %
Efficiency      = 400 / 500       = 80 %
At 1 Mbps: 500 x 8 = 4000 bits -> 4 ms (only 3.2 ms carry the message)
Trap: 100 / 400 = 25 % divides by the message, not by what is sent

Common slips: only the data link layer adds a trailer (the FCS) as well as a header; the TCP/IP model has no separate session or presentation layer; SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are prohibited (RFC 6176 and RFC 7568), so name TLS for encryption today; and ARP and OSPF are not carried over UDP or TCP, while RIP, BGP, DHCP and DNS are.

notes.text: Remember the OSI layers from bottom to top with 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' (Physical, Data link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application), and match each layer with its PDU: bit, frame, packet, segment, data.

Textbooks differ on TCP/IP: many describe 4 layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) while Forouzan uses 5 (Application, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical). Read the options carefully before choosing the layer count.
Encryption and compression belong to the OSI presentation layer, and dialogue control and checkpointing to the session layer; in TCP/IP both jobs are absorbed into the application layer.

flashcards.front: What are the three key elements of a protocol?
flashcards.back: Syntax (format of the data), semantics (meaning of each field and action to take) and timing (when and how fast to send).

flashcards.front: Which OSI layers map to the TCP/IP application layer?
flashcards.back: The OSI application, presentation and session layers (7, 6 and 5) are all folded into the TCP/IP application layer.

flashcards.front: Name the four levels of addressing in TCP/IP and the layer each belongs to.
flashcards.back: Physical (MAC) at the data link layer, logical (IP) at the network layer, port at the transport layer, and specific (e.g. e-mail address or URL) at the application layer.

questions.questionText: How many dedicated duplex links are required to connect 8 devices in a fully connected mesh topology?
questions.explanation: A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links; for n = 8 that is 8 x 7 / 2 = 28. 56 is the total number of ports and 7 is the ports per device.

questions.questionText: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for routing packets from the source network to the destination network?
questions.explanation: The network layer (layer 3) handles logical (IP) addressing and chooses the path through intermediate routers. The data link layer only moves frames across a single link.

questions.questionText: How many layers does the TCP/IP reference model have in its standard form (RFC 1122)?
questions.explanation: RFC 1122 describes four layers: application, transport, internet and link (network access). Some textbooks, such as Forouzan, split the link layer into data link and physical and draw five.

questions.questionText: In the OSI reference model, which layer is responsible for data encryption and compression?
questions.explanation: The presentation layer (layer 6) handles the representation of data: translation, compression and encryption. In the TCP/IP model these jobs are done inside the application layer, for example by a TLS library.

questions.questionText: In which topology are all devices connected to one central node, so that a failure of that node brings down the whole network?
questions.explanation: In a star each device has its own link to a central hub or switch. A cable fault affects only one device, but the central device is a single point of failure.

questions.questionText: Which of the following describes full-duplex communication?
options: Data flows in both directions at the same time
Data flows in one direction only
Data flows in both directions, but only one direction at a time
Data is buffered and retransmitted later
questions.explanation: Full-duplex lets both stations transmit simultaneously, like a telephone call. One direction only is simplex, and taking turns in both directions is half-duplex, like a walkie-talkie.

questions.questionText: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks and default gateways to hosts on a network?
questions.explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) leases addresses and settings to clients; it is an application-layer protocol over UDP ports 67 (server) and 68 (client). ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses and DNS maps names to IP addresses.

questions.questionText: When TCP is the transport protocol, what is the protocol data unit at the transport layer called?
questions.explanation: TCP carries data in segments (UDP's unit is the user datagram). The network-layer PDU is the packet or datagram, the data link PDU the frame, and the physical layer carries bits.

questions.questionText: Which organisation develops the Internet's protocol standards and publishes them as RFCs (Requests for Comments)?
questions.explanation: The Internet Engineering Task Force develops Internet standards, published as RFCs such as RFC 791 (IPv4) and RFC 9293 (TCP). IEEE writes LAN standards such as 802.3, and ITU-T writes telecommunication standards.

questions.questionText: In the memory aid 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for the OSI layers from layer 7 down to layer 1, which layer does the word 'Need' stand for?
questions.explanation: Read top down: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical. 'Need' is the fifth word, so it is the network layer (layer 3).

questions.questionText: Which TCP/IP protocol do hosts and routers use to report delivery problems, such as 'destination unreachable', back to the source of an IP datagram?
questions.explanation: ICMP (RFC 792) carries error-reporting and query messages inside IP datagrams, with protocol number 1. ARP resolves addresses, and TCP and UDP are transport protocols.

questions.questionText: Which element of a protocol specifies when data should be sent and how fast it may be sent?
questions.explanation: A protocol has three key elements: syntax (the format and order of fields), semantics (the meaning of each field and the action to take) and timing (when to send and at what speed).

questions.questionText: HTTP was used by the first Web browsers and servers and was widely adopted before any formal standard existed. A standard that arises in this way is called:
questions.explanation: A de facto standard ('in fact') is established by widespread use without formal approval, while a de jure standard ('by law') is formally adopted by a recognised body. HTTP was later specified in IETF RFCs.

questions.questionText: Which IEEE 802 working group standardises wireless personal area networks (WPANs)?
questions.explanation: IEEE 802.15 covers WPANs: 802.15.1 was based on Bluetooth and 802.15.4 underlies Zigbee. 802.3 is Ethernet, 802.11 is wireless LAN and 802.1 covers bridging and VLANs.

questions.questionText: The application layer of the TCP/IP model corresponds to the OSI application layer together with which two other OSI layers?
questions.explanation: TCP/IP's application layer absorbs OSI layers 5, 6 and 7, so session control, encryption and data formatting are handled by the applications themselves. The transport layer maps one-to-one onto OSI layer 4.

questions.questionText: During encapsulation, which layer adds both a header and a trailer to the data it receives from the layer above?
questions.explanation: The data link layer adds a header (MAC addresses and type) and a trailer (the frame check sequence, a CRC) to form a frame. The transport and network layers add headers only.

questions.questionText: Which pairing of address type and TCP/IP layer is correct?
questions.explanation: Port numbers (16 bits) identify processes at the transport layer. MAC addresses belong to the data link layer, IP addresses to the network layer, and URLs or e-mail addresses are application-level (specific) addresses.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the type of service offered by layers of the TCP/IP model is correct?
options: The Internet layer offers only connectionless service, while the transport layer offers both connection-oriented (TCP) and connectionless (UDP) service
The Internet layer offers both connection-oriented and connectionless service, while the transport layer offers only connection-oriented service
Both the Internet layer and the transport layer offer only connection-oriented service
The Internet layer is connection-oriented, while the transport layer offers only connectionless service
questions.explanation: IP is a connectionless datagram service, and above it the transport layer offers a choice of TCP (connection-oriented, reliable) or UDP (connectionless). The second option is the pattern Tanenbaum gives for the OSI model (both services at the network layer, only connection-oriented service at the transport layer), not for TCP/IP.

questions.questionText: Which function belongs to the OSI data link layer rather than to the network layer?
options: Choosing a path through several intermediate networks
Assigning logical addresses that are unique across the internetwork
Delivering frames between two directly connected nodes using MAC addresses
Fragmenting packets to fit the MTU of the next network
questions.explanation: The data link layer gives hop-to-hop (node-to-node) delivery of frames over one link. Routing, logical addressing and IPv4 fragmentation are network-layer jobs.

questions.questionText: Which of the following protocols is carried directly inside IP datagrams rather than over TCP or UDP?
questions.explanation: OSPF messages are placed straight into IP datagrams with protocol number 89. RIP uses UDP port 520, BGP uses TCP port 179 and DNS normally uses UDP (or TCP) port 53.

questions.questionText: Which protocol's messages are carried directly in an Ethernet frame, with no IP header at all?
questions.explanation: ARP requests and replies use EtherType 0x0806 and sit directly in the frame, because ARP is how a host finds the MAC address it needs. ICMP and OSPF travel inside IP datagrams, and DHCP runs over UDP and IP.

questions.questionText: In a layered network architecture, what is the difference between a protocol and an interface?
options: A protocol is the set of rules between peer layers on different machines; an interface defines the operations and services between adjacent layers on the same machine
A protocol connects adjacent layers on one machine; an interface connects peer layers on different machines
A protocol is always implemented in hardware; an interface is always implemented in software
A protocol applies only to the physical layer; interfaces apply to all the other layers
questions.explanation: Layer n on one host communicates logically with layer n on the other host using the layer-n protocol, and it obtains services from layer n-1 on the same host through the interface. Keeping the two separate lets one layer's implementation change without affecting its neighbours.

questions.questionText: In the OSI service model with the four primitives request, indication, response and confirm, which primitive informs the called service user that a remote peer wants to set up a connection?
questions.explanation: The caller issues CONNECT.request; the service provider delivers CONNECT.indication to the called user; the called user answers with CONNECT.response; and the caller finally receives CONNECT.confirm.

questions.questionText: Which analogy best matches a connectionless (datagram) service?
options: A telephone call, in which a circuit is set up before anyone talks
The postal system, in which each letter carries the full destination address and is handled independently
A pipe, in which items always come out in the order they went in
A train carriage reserved for one passenger for the whole journey
questions.explanation: In a connectionless service every message carries the full address and is forwarded on its own, so messages may take different paths and arrive out of order. A connection-oriented service works like a telephone call, with setup, transfer and release.

questions.questionText: In a bus topology, what is the purpose of the terminators fitted at both ends of the backbone cable?
options: To amplify the signal for distant stations
To assign addresses to the stations on the bus
To connect the bus to a router
To absorb the signal at the cable ends so that it does not reflect back and interfere
questions.explanation: A terminator is a resistor matched to the cable's impedance. Without it the signal reflects off the open end and corrupts later transmissions, disrupting the whole bus.

questions.questionText: A protocol stack has 4 layers and each layer adds a 20-byte header. An application passes down a 560-byte message, which is sent on a 1 Mbps link (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s, no other overhead). What fraction of the transmitted bytes are headers, and how long does the transmission take?
questions.explanation: Headers = 4 x 20 = 80 bytes, so 640 bytes are sent and the header fraction is 80 / 640 = 12.5 %. Time = 640 x 8 / 10^6 = 5.12 ms; 14.3 % and 4.48 ms wrongly use the 560-byte message alone.

questions.questionText: A web server sends 1,200 bytes of application data in one TCP segment over IPv4 and Ethernet. Assuming 20-byte TCP and IPv4 headers (no options), a 14-byte Ethernet header and a 4-byte FCS, how long is the Ethernet frame from the destination MAC address to the end of the FCS?
questions.explanation: Frame = 1200 + 20 (TCP) + 20 (IPv4) + 14 (header) + 4 (FCS) = 1,258 bytes. 1,240 is only the IP packet, 1,254 forgets the FCS and 1,266 wrongly adds the 8-byte preamble and SFD.

questions.questionText: A host sends a long file over 100 Mbps Ethernet in full-size frames with a 1,500-byte payload. Each frame also costs 8 bytes of preamble and SFD, a 14-byte header, a 4-byte FCS and a 12-byte inter-frame gap, and every payload carries 20-byte IPv4 and 20-byte TCP headers (no options). What is the maximum application-data throughput (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s)?
questions.explanation: Each frame occupies 8 + 14 + 1500 + 4 + 12 = 1,538 byte times and carries 1500 - 40 = 1,460 bytes of data, so throughput = 100 x 1460 / 1538 = 94.9 Mbps. 97.5 ignores the TCP/IP headers and 96.2 ignores the preamble and gap.

questions.questionText: A fully connected mesh network uses 66 dedicated duplex links. How many devices does it have, and how many I/O ports are needed in total?
questions.explanation: n(n - 1)/2 = 66 gives n = 12. Each device needs n - 1 = 11 ports, so the total is 12 x 11 = 132 (two ports per link: 2 x 66); 66 ports counts only one end of each link.

questions.questionText: A host receives an Ethernet frame whose EtherType is 0x0800. Inside it, the IPv4 Protocol field is 17 and the transport header's destination port is 53. Which chain of protocols processes the frame, from bottom to top?
questions.explanation: EtherType 0x0800 means IPv4 (0x86DD would be IPv6 and 0x0806 ARP), Protocol 17 means UDP (6 would be TCP), and port 53 is DNS. Each header names the protocol that receives its payload.

questions.questionText: A packet travels from host A through two routers to host B, and no NAT is used. Which statement correctly describes the addresses carried on the three links?
options: The MAC addresses stay the same on every link, while the IP addresses change at each router
Both the MAC and the IP addresses stay the same from end to end
The source and destination IP addresses stay the same on every link, while the source and destination MAC addresses change on each link
Both the MAC and the IP addresses are replaced at each router
questions.explanation: IP addresses identify the two end hosts and are carried unchanged across the internetwork. Each router removes the incoming frame and builds a new one whose source MAC is its outgoing interface and whose destination MAC is the next hop, found by ARP.

subtopics.subtitle: Repeaters to gateways by OSI layer, forwarding basis, and counting collision/broadcast domains

concepts.text: Connecting Devices by Layer

Connecting devices are classified by the highest OSI layer they understand. Physical-layer devices (repeaters, hubs) only see bits, data-link devices (bridges, switches) read frame MAC addresses, network-layer devices (routers) read IP addresses, and gateways can work up to the application layer. The higher the layer, the more intelligent the forwarding decision and the more traffic the device can isolate.
Physical-layer devices regenerate and repeat bits without examining addresses:
items: Repeater: receives a weakened or corrupted signal and regenerates the original bit pattern before retransmitting it, extending the physical length of a LAN segment. It regenerates rather than amplifies, so noise is not amplified.

Hub: a multiport repeater. A frame arriving on one port is broadcast out of every other port, so all attached stations share the bandwidth and form a single collision domain, which causes congestion as the network grows.
Hubs operate half-duplex and cannot filter traffic; a passive hub simply joins wires, while an active hub also regenerates the signal.

concepts.text: Bridges

A bridge operates at the physical and data link layers and connects two (or a few) LAN segments. It keeps a table of MAC addresses and ports: a frame whose destination is on the same segment it arrived from is filtered (dropped), otherwise it is forwarded only to the correct segment, and frames with an unknown destination are flooded. A transparent (learning) bridge builds its table automatically by recording the source MAC address and incoming port of every frame, so stations are unaware of it. Because redundant bridges create loops in which broadcasts circulate forever, bridges run the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D), which blocks redundant ports to form a loop-free tree.
Switches

A layer-2 switch is essentially a fast multiport bridge implemented in hardware. It learns MAC addresses into a MAC address (CAM) table and delivers each frame only to the port of the destination, so every port is a separate collision domain and full-duplex links remove collisions entirely. All ports still belong to one broadcast domain: broadcasts and unknown unicasts are flooded to every port.
Switching methods and extensions to know:
items: Store-and-forward: receives the entire frame and checks the CRC before forwarding; higher latency but drops corrupt frames.
Cut-through: starts forwarding as soon as the destination MAC (first 6 bytes after the preamble) is read; lowest latency but forwards errored frames.
Fragment-free: reads the first 64 bytes before forwarding, filtering most collision fragments (runts).
VLAN (IEEE 802.1Q): logically divides one switch into several broadcast domains, each behaving like a separate LAN.
Layer-3 switch: a switch that also routes between VLANs or subnets using IP addresses at hardware speed.

concepts.text: Routers and Other Devices

A router works at layers 1 to 3 and connects different networks (for example a LAN to a WAN or to the Internet). It forwards packets using the destination IP address and a routing table built statically by an administrator or dynamically by routing protocols such as RIP, OSPF and BGP. Every router interface belongs to a different network, so a router separates both collision domains and broadcast domains; it does not forward broadcasts by default. Routers also choose best paths, decrement TTL and can filter traffic with access control lists.
Other devices commonly found in a network:
items: Gateway: operates up to the application layer and translates between networks that use different protocol stacks or formats (e.g. an e-mail or VoIP gateway); in TCP/IP the term 'default gateway' simply means the router a host uses to leave its subnet.
Modem (modulator-demodulator): converts digital data to analog signals for telephone or cable lines and back, e.g. DSL and cable modems.
Wireless access point (AP): a layer-2 device that bridges 802.11 wireless stations onto a wired Ethernet LAN.
NIC (network interface card): gives a host its physical connection and its unique 48-bit MAC address; it works at layers 1 and 2.
Brouter: a combined bridge and router that routes routable protocols and bridges the rest.

concepts.text: Worked Example: Counting Domains

A router R has two interfaces in use. Interface 1 connects to switch S; S also connects three PCs directly and one hub H1 that has four PCs. Interface 2 connects to hub H2 with six PCs. Collision domains: each used switch port is one domain, so S gives 5 (link to R, three PCs, the H1 segment with its four PCs); H2 and its link to R form 1 more, so the total is 6. Broadcast domains: only the router splits them, so there are 2, one per router interface.

concepts.plainText: Broadcast domains = number of router interfaces in use (without VLANs)

concepts.text: Going Deeper: How Devices Learn, Filter and Forward
A quick picture of each device, with an everyday analogy:
items: Hub (layer 1), the least intelligent device: whatever arrives on one port is repeated out of all the others, like shouting in a room where everyone hears. All ports share one collision domain, so every added station adds congestion, and a hub is never faster than a switch.

Bridge (layer 2): joins two LAN segments and passes a frame across only when the destination MAC address is on the other side, like a doorkeeper between two rooms who carries a note through only if the addressee is in the other room. Each side becomes its own collision domain.

Switch (layer 2), a 'smart hub' or multiport bridge: sends each unicast frame only to the port of its destination MAC address, like whispering directly to one person, and lets every port run full-duplex at full speed.
Router (layer 3): joins different networks and forwards packets by destination IP address, making a path decision for each packet, like a post office sorting mail for different cities.
Memory line: hub = repeat to all; switch = direct delivery by MAC; router = between networks by IP.
A home 'Wi-Fi router' is several devices in one box: a router with NAT, a small Ethernet switch, a wireless access point and a DHCP server, and often a DSL, cable or fibre modem too.

concepts.text: A learning switch or bridge runs the same procedure for every frame. It first records the frame's source MAC address against the arrival port, with a timestamp. It then looks up the destination: a broadcast or an unknown unicast is flooded out of every port except the arrival port, a destination learned on the arrival port is filtered (dropped), and any other known destination is forwarded out of just its own port. Entries that are not refreshed within the ageing time (300 s by default in IEEE 802.1D) are deleted, so a station that moves is relearned at its new port.

rows: Flood to all ports except the arrival port (within the VLAN)
Unicast not yet in the MAC table
Flood to all ports except the arrival port
Unicast learned on the arrival port
Filter: discard, the segment already delivered it
Forward out of that one port only
Any frame failing the FCS check (store-and-forward)

concepts.text:
Worked trace 1: 4-port switch, empty table; A on port 1, B on 2, C on 3, D on 4
Frame        Learns   Destination known?   Action
1  A -> B    A = 1    no                   flood to 2, 3, 4
2  B -> A    B = 2    yes (port 1)         forward to 1
3  C -> A    C = 3    yes (port 1)         forward to 1
4  A -> D    (A)      no                   flood to 2, 3, 4
5  D -> all  D = 4    broadcast            flood to 1, 2, 3
6  A -> D    (A)      yes (port 4)         forward to 4
Final table: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4; 3 of the 6 frames were flooded

A router treats each packet quite differently. It removes the layer-2 frame, checks the IPv4 header and looks up the destination IP address in its routing table using the longest-prefix match. It then decrements TTL (discarding the packet and sending ICMP Time Exceeded if TTL reaches 0), recomputes the header checksum, uses ARP to find the next hop's MAC address and sends the packet in a brand-new frame. Limited broadcasts (255.255.255.255) are never forwarded, which is why every router interface bounds a broadcast domain.

concepts.plainText: Store-and-forward over N links (N - 1 switches): d = N x L/R; cut-through: d is about L/R + (N - 1) x h/R, where h bits are read before forwarding starts (propagation, queueing and processing ignored)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: 1,000-byte frame, 2 switches (3 links), 1 Gbps links
L/R = 8,000 bits / 10^9 bit/s                 = 8 µs per link
Store-and-forward: each switch waits for the whole frame
  d = 3 x 8 µs                                = 24 µs
Cut-through: forward after the 6-byte destination MAC
  h/R = 48 bits / 10^9 bit/s                   = 0.048 µs per switch
  d = 8 + 2 x 0.048                            = 8.096 µs
Propagation, queueing, processing and preamble ignored

Worked example 3: counting domains with VLANs
24-port switch: VLAN 10 = ports 1-8, VLAN 20 = 9-16, VLAN 30 = 17-22
Ports 1-7: one PC each; port 8: a hub with 5 PCs
Ports 9-16 and 17-22: one PC each; port 23: trunk to a router
Port 24: unused
Collision domains = used ports = 7 + 1 (hub segment) + 8 + 6 + 1 = 23
Broadcast domains = VLANs = 3 (the router routes between them)
Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D) in brief:
items: Every switch has a bridge ID made of a priority (default 32768) followed by its MAC address. The lowest bridge ID wins the root-bridge election, so priority is compared first and the MAC address only breaks ties.
Each non-root switch chooses one root port, its port with the lowest total path cost to the root; each LAN segment gets one designated port; all remaining ports are blocked.
Port costs fall with link speed (802.1D-1998 values: 100 for 10 Mbps, 19 for 100 Mbps, 4 for 1 Gbps), so faster paths are preferred.
Classic STP moves a port through blocking, listening, learning and forwarding, taking 30 to 50 s; Rapid STP (802.1w) converges in a few seconds or less.

concepts.text: Common mistakes: bridges and switches do not split broadcast domains (only routers or VLANs do); a layer-2 switch forwards by MAC address, never by IP; a repeater regenerates the bit pattern instead of amplifying the analog signal and its noise; a hub is not faster than a switch, because its ports share one half-duplex collision domain; and a basic bridge does not translate between protocols.

For domain counting, give one collision domain to every link or segment that ends at a switch, bridge or router port (a hub and everything on it is one segment), and one broadcast domain to every router interface or VLAN in use.

formulas.plainText: Collision domains on a switch = number of ports in use
Broadcast domains = router interfaces in use (without VLANs)
A hub with n ports forms a single collision domain

notes.text: Quick rule: a hub gives 1 collision and 1 broadcast domain; an n-port switch gives n collision domains and 1 broadcast domain; a router gives one collision and one broadcast domain per interface.
Bridges and switches do not stop broadcasts; they flood broadcast and unknown-destination frames to all ports. Only routers (or VLANs on a switch) break up broadcast domains.
A switch is often called a multiport bridge and a hub a multiport repeater; MCQs often test this pairing along with the layer of each device.

formulas.title: Switch collision domains
formulas.plainText: Collision domains = switch ports in use
formulas.description: Every switch or bridge port that has a device or segment attached is its own collision domain.

formulas.title: Broadcast domains
formulas.plainText: Broadcast domains = router interfaces in use
formulas.description: Without VLANs, only router interfaces split broadcast domains, so each active interface is one broadcast domain.

formulas.title: Hub collision domain
formulas.plainText: Collision domains of a hub = 1
formulas.description: All ports of a hub share one medium, so however many ports it has, it forms a single collision domain.

flashcards.front: How does a transparent (learning) bridge build its forwarding table?
flashcards.back: It records the source MAC address and arrival port of every frame it receives; unknown destinations are flooded until they are learned.
Store-and-forward buffers the whole frame and checks the CRC before forwarding; cut-through forwards as soon as the destination MAC is read, giving lower latency but passing on errored frames.

flashcards.front: Why do bridges and switches run the Spanning Tree Protocol?
flashcards.back: Redundant links create loops in which broadcast frames circulate endlessly; STP (IEEE 802.1D) blocks redundant ports to form a loop-free tree.

questions.questionText: Which of these devices works only at the physical layer (layer 1), handling signals without reading any addresses?
questions.explanation: A hub only repeats signals (bits) out of every port and never reads addresses, so it is a layer-1 device. Bridges and switches read MAC addresses (layer 2), and routers read IP addresses (layer 3).

questions.questionText: A router operates at which layer of the OSI model?
questions.explanation: A router forwards packets by their destination IP (logical) address using a routing table, which is a network-layer (layer 3) function.

questions.questionText: What is the main difference between a hub and a switch?
options: A switch sends a unicast frame only out of the port leading to its destination, while a hub repeats it out of every port
A hub is faster because it does not examine frames
A switch forwards frames by IP address
A hub operates at the network layer
questions.explanation: A switch learns which MAC address is on which port and delivers each unicast frame only there, whereas a hub repeats every signal to all ports. A hub is not faster: all of its ports share one half-duplex collision domain.

questions.questionText: Which device regenerates a weakened signal and retransmits it, extending the length of a LAN segment at the physical layer?
questions.explanation: A repeater receives a weak or noisy signal, regenerates the original bit pattern and sends it on. It works only at layer 1 and does not filter any traffic.

questions.questionText: A hub is also known as a:
questions.explanation: A hub regenerates the incoming signal and repeats it out of every other port, which is what a repeater does, so it is called a multiport repeater. The multiport bridge is the switch.

questions.questionText: Which device connects IEEE 802.11 wireless stations to a wired Ethernet LAN?
questions.explanation: An access point is a layer-2 device that bridges frames between the 802.11 wireless cell and the wired Ethernet.

questions.questionText: What is the job of a modem?
options: To route packets between networks by IP address
To learn MAC addresses and forward frames
To translate domain names into IP addresses
To convert digital data into analog signals for transmission and back again at the receiver
questions.explanation: Modem stands for modulator-demodulator: it modulates digital data onto an analog carrier (telephone line, cable or radio) and demodulates it at the far end. Routing, switching and name resolution are done by other devices and protocols.

questions.questionText: A network interface card (NIC) operates at which OSI layers?
questions.explanation: A NIC drives the medium (layer 1) and builds and checks frames carrying its own 48-bit MAC address (layer 2). IP processing is done by the host's operating system, not by the card.

questions.questionText: Which device is typically used to join two LAN segments and filters frames by MAC address, so that local traffic stays on its own segment?
questions.explanation: A bridge learns which MAC addresses are on each side and forwards a frame across only when its destination is on the other segment, splitting the collision domain in two.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly contrasts a layer-2 switch with a router?
options: Switches operate at the network layer, while routers operate at the data link layer
Routers forward packets using IP addresses, while switches forward frames using MAC addresses
Switches forward packets between different networks, while routers forward only within a single network
Routers amplify signals, while switches do not
questions.explanation: A layer-2 switch forwards frames inside one LAN using its MAC address table, whereas a router forwards packets between different networks using the destination IP address and its routing table.

questions.questionText: Which networking device breaks up collision domains but keeps all of its ports in one broadcast domain (with no VLANs configured)?
questions.explanation: Each switch port is its own collision domain, but broadcasts are flooded to every port, so the whole switch is one broadcast domain. A router splits both kinds of domain, while a hub or repeater splits neither.

questions.questionText: How does a transparent (learning) switch build its MAC address table?
options: It records the destination MAC address of each frame it forwards
It sends ARP requests to every host when it starts
The administrator must enter every address manually
It records the source MAC address of each incoming frame together with the port it arrived on
questions.explanation: Backward learning uses the source address: a frame from MAC X arriving on port p shows that X is reachable through p. A destination address says nothing about where that station is, and ARP is a host protocol for IP-to-MAC mapping.

questions.questionText: A switch receives a unicast frame whose destination MAC address is not yet in its MAC address table. What does it do?
options: Sends the frame back out of the port it arrived on
Floods the frame out of every port except the one it arrived on
Holds the frame until the destination sends a frame of its own
questions.explanation: An unknown unicast is flooded to all other ports in the same VLAN. When the destination replies, the switch learns its port, and later frames to it are forwarded only there.

questions.questionText: A switch has learned that both the source and the destination MAC addresses of a frame are on port 3, which connects to a hub. What does the switch do when the frame arrives on port 3?
options: Filters (discards) it, because the hub has already delivered it to the destination
Sends it back out of port 3
Floods it out of all ports
Forwards it out of the port that leads to the router
questions.explanation: The hub already repeated the frame to every station on that segment, including the destination, so the switch filters it rather than wasting bandwidth on its other links.

questions.questionText: A router receives an Ethernet frame carrying an IPv4 packet addressed to the limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255. What does it do?
options: Forwards it out of all its other interfaces
Processes it itself if it is relevant, but does not forward it to other networks
Forwards it only along the default route
Sends it back to the source with an ICMP error
questions.explanation: Routers never forward limited broadcasts (RFC 1812), which is why each router interface is the edge of a broadcast domain. The router may still read the packet itself, for example a DHCP request on that segment.

questions.questionText: Which switching method receives the entire frame and checks its FCS before forwarding it?
questions.explanation: Store-and-forward buffers the whole frame and verifies the CRC, so corrupted frames are dropped, at the cost of a delay proportional to frame length. Cut-through forwards after reading the destination MAC address, and fragment-free after the first 64 bytes.

questions.questionText: Why does a fragment-free switch wait for the first 64 bytes of a frame before forwarding it?
options: Any collision on a correctly sized Ethernet occurs within the first 64 bytes (the minimum frame size), so a frame that gets that far is not a collision fragment
The frame check sequence always lies within the first 64 bytes, so errors can be checked early
The source and destination IP addresses of the packet end at byte 64 of the frame
The switch needs the first 64 bytes to add or remove an 802.1Q VLAN tag
questions.explanation: Collision fragments (runts) are shorter than 64 bytes because, on a correctly sized half-duplex network, any collision happens within the first 512 bit times. Waiting for 64 bytes filters most runts while keeping latency well below store-and-forward.

questions.questionText: What problem does the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D) solve in a switched LAN with redundant links?
options: It encrypts frames sent between switches so that redundant links cannot be tapped
It assigns IP addresses to the switches so that they can be managed remotely
It prevents layer-2 loops, which would cause broadcast storms and unstable MAC tables, by blocking redundant ports
It spreads traffic equally over all the redundant links to add bandwidth
questions.explanation: Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a broadcast caught in a loop circulates and multiplies without end. STP builds a loop-free tree by blocking some ports and re-enables them if an active link fails.

questions.questionText: An administrator splits one 24-port switch into VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. Which statement is correct?
options: Broadcasts still reach all 24 ports, but unicasts are separated
A broadcast from a VLAN 10 port reaches only VLAN 10 ports, and traffic between the VLANs must pass through a router or layer-3 switch
Hosts in the two VLANs can exchange frames directly because they share the same switch
The VLANs reduce the switch to two collision domains
questions.explanation: Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain, so frames never cross between VLANs at layer 2 and inter-VLAN traffic has to be routed. Every port remains its own collision domain.

questions.questionText: What distinguishes a layer-3 switch from an ordinary layer-2 switch?
options: It has more ports, but it still forwards every frame by MAC address only
It works only at the physical layer, regenerating the signal on each port
It connects only wireless devices, acting as an access point controller
It can also route packets between VLANs or subnets by IP address, in hardware at switching speed
questions.explanation: A layer-3 (multilayer) switch combines MAC-based switching with IP routing, usually in hardware, and is typically used for fast inter-VLAN routing inside a campus network.

questions.questionText: Which device can work up to the application layer and translates between networks that use completely different protocol stacks, for example between an e-mail system and an SMS service?
questions.explanation: A gateway (protocol converter) understands the layers of both stacks and converts messages between them. In TCP/IP, 'default gateway' simply means the router that a host uses to leave its own subnet.

questions.questionText: When an IPv4 router forwards a packet (no NAT, no IP options), which header field does it always change?
questions.explanation: The router decrements TTL by 1 (dropping the packet and sending ICMP Time Exceeded if it reaches 0) and so must also recompute the header checksum. Without NAT the addresses and the Protocol field are unchanged.

questions.questionText: A typical home 'Wi-Fi router' box supplied by an ISP usually combines which functions?
options: Only a layer-1 hub that repeats signals between the wired devices
Only a wireless repeater that extends a neighbouring network
A DNS root server and a mail server for the household
A router with NAT, a small Ethernet switch, a wireless access point and a DHCP server
questions.explanation: The box routes between the home LAN and the ISP (with NAT), switches between its LAN ports, bridges Wi-Fi clients as an access point and hands out addresses by DHCP; many also contain the DSL, cable or fibre modem.

questions.questionText: Why is CSMA/CD not needed on a full-duplex link between a host and a switch port?
options: The switch retransmits every frame twice, so collisions do not matter
Each end has its own path for sending and receiving on a dedicated link, so collisions cannot occur
Full-duplex links use token passing instead
The host sends only when the switch polls it
questions.explanation: On a point-to-point full-duplex link each direction has its own channel with a single transmitter, so there is no shared medium to collide on. CSMA/CD is needed only on shared half-duplex segments such as a hub.

questions.questionText: A router has three interfaces in use. Interface 1 connects to a switch that also has 9 PCs on 9 other ports; interface 2 connects to a hub with 6 PCs; interface 3 connects to a second switch that has 4 PCs and one hub (with 3 PCs) on its other ports. With no VLANs, how many collision domains and broadcast domains are there?
questions.explanation: Switch 1 gives 10 (router link + 9 PCs), the hub on interface 2 gives 1, and switch 2 gives 6 (router link + 4 PCs + the hub segment): 10 + 1 + 6 = 17. Each router interface is one broadcast domain, so there are 3.

questions.questionText: A 24-port switch has VLAN 10 on ports 1-10 and VLAN 20 on ports 11-20; ports 21-24 are unused, with nothing connected. Ports 1-9 and 11-20 each have one PC, and port 10 connects a hub with 4 PCs. How many collision domains and broadcast domains are there?
questions.explanation: Every used switch port is one collision domain: 10 + 10 = 20 (the hub and its 4 PCs share port 10's domain, and the empty ports 21-24 count for nothing). Each VLAN in use is one broadcast domain, so there are 2; 1 would ignore the VLANs.

questions.questionText: A 4-port switch starts with an empty MAC table; A is on port 1, B on port 2, C on port 3 and D on port 4. The frames sent are: A to B, C to D, B to A, A to D, D to C, A to D. How many of the six frames are flooded, and how many entries does the table hold afterwards (no ageing)?
questions.explanation: A to B is flooded (B unknown), C to D is flooded (D unknown), B to A is forwarded, A to D is flooded (D still unknown), then D to C teaches D and the last A to D is forwarded: 3 floods. Learning source addresses gives A, C, B and D, so 4 entries.

questions.questionText: A 1,250-byte frame travels from host A to host B through 2 store-and-forward switches, and all three links run at 10 Mbps. Ignoring propagation, queueing and processing delays, how long after A starts sending does B receive the last bit (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s)?
questions.explanation: One link takes L/R = 10,000 bits / 10^7 bit/s = 1 ms, and each switch must receive the whole frame before sending it on, so the delay is 3 links x 1 ms = 3 ms. 0.375 ms treats 1,250 bytes as bits.

questions.questionText: Host A sends a 1,500-byte frame to host B through 3 switches over 4 links of 100 Mbps. What is the end-to-end delay with store-and-forward switches, and with cut-through switches that start forwarding after reading the 6-byte destination MAC address? Ignore preamble, propagation, queueing and processing (1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s).
questions.explanation: L/R = 12,000 / 10^8 = 120 µs, so store-and-forward takes 4 x 120 = 480 µs. Cut-through adds only 48 bits / 10^8 = 0.48 µs per switch: 120 + 3 x 0.48 = 121.44 µs.

questions.questionText: Four switches run STP. S1: priority 32768, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:01; S2: priority 32768, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:05; S3: priority 4096, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:09; S4: priority 4096, MAC 00:1A:2B:00:00:07. Which switch becomes the root bridge?
questions.explanation: The lowest bridge ID wins, and the priority is compared first: S3 and S4 tie at 4096, so the lower MAC address breaks the tie and S4 (...:07) becomes root. S1 has the lowest MAC but a higher priority.

subtopics.title: Transmission Media
subtopics.subtitle: Twisted pair, coax, fibre and wireless; impairments, Nyquist, Shannon and delays

concepts.text: Guided vs Unguided Media

Transmission media sit below the physical layer and carry signals between devices. Guided (wired) media confine the signal to a physical path: twisted-pair and coaxial cable carry electrical signals, and optical fibre carries light. Unguided (wireless) media broadcast electromagnetic waves through air or space without a physical conductor: radio waves, microwaves and infrared. Choice depends on bandwidth, distance, cost, noise immunity, security and ease of installation.
Copper cables in practice:
items: Twisted pair: two insulated copper wires twisted together so that interference and crosstalk induced in the two wires cancel; terminated with RJ-45 connectors and limited to about 100 m per Ethernet segment.
UTP (unshielded twisted pair) is cheap and flexible and dominates LANs; STP (shielded twisted pair) adds a metal foil or braid for better noise immunity at higher cost and stiffness.

Coaxial cable: a central copper conductor, insulator, braided outer conductor (shield) and jacket; higher bandwidth and better shielding than twisted pair. RG-59/RG-6 carry cable TV, RG-58 was thin Ethernet (10Base2, 185 m) and RG-8 thick Ethernet (10Base5, 500 m), using BNC connectors.

rows: 1 Gbps (10 Gbps up to about 55 m)

concepts.text: Optical Fibre

Optical fibre guides light through a thin glass or plastic core surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. When light strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle, it undergoes total internal reflection and stays inside the core, travelling long distances with very little loss. A light source (LED or laser) at the transmitter and a photodiode at the receiver convert between electrical and optical signals.
Fibre modes, advantages and drawbacks:
items: Multimode: wider core (50 or 62.5 micrometres), many light paths, LED source; modal dispersion limits it to short distances (hundreds of metres to about 2 km). Step-index has a sharp core boundary; graded-index gradually lowers the index to reduce dispersion.
Single-mode: very narrow core (about 8-10 micrometres), one path, laser source; lowest dispersion, used for long-haul links of tens to hundreds of kilometres.
Advantages: very high bandwidth, low attenuation, immunity to electromagnetic interference, light weight, and difficult to tap (better security).
Disadvantages: higher installation cost, needs skilled splicing, fragile, and light travels in one direction so a duplex link needs two fibres.

concepts.text: Unguided (Wireless) Media
Wireless media are grouped by frequency band:
items: Radio waves (about 3 kHz to 1 GHz): omnidirectional, travel long distances and penetrate walls; used for AM/FM radio, TV and paging, but prone to interference.
Microwaves (1 to 300 GHz): unidirectional, need line of sight between dish or horn antennas and relay towers roughly every 50 km; used for cellular, terrestrial links, Wi-Fi and satellite.
Infrared (300 GHz to 400 THz): very short range, line of sight, cannot penetrate walls, so it does not interfere between rooms; used in remote controls and IrDA.
Satellite: a microwave relay in orbit; a geostationary satellite at about 35,786 km covers a third of the Earth, but the up-and-down path adds roughly 240-270 ms of propagation delay.

rows: Line of sight / a few metres

concepts.text: Impairments, Bandwidth and Data Rate

Signals are degraded by three impairments. Attenuation is loss of energy with distance, measured in decibels and compensated by amplifiers or repeaters. Distortion is change of signal shape because different frequency components travel at different speeds. Noise is unwanted energy: thermal (random electron motion), induced (from motors and appliances), crosstalk (from adjacent wires) and impulse (spikes from lightning or power lines). Bandwidth in hertz is the range of frequencies a channel passes; together with the number of signal levels and the signal-to-noise ratio it limits the data rate in bits per second.

concepts.plainText: Nyquist bit rate = 2 x B x log2(L), B = bandwidth in Hz, L = number of signal levels
Shannon capacity = B x log2(1 + SNR), SNR as a ratio, not in dB

concepts.text: Transmission delay is the time to push all bits of a frame onto the link, L/R, and depends on frame length and bandwidth; propagation delay is the time for one bit to travel the link, d/v, and depends on distance and signal speed (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in copper or fibre). Example: a 2,500-byte (20,000-bit) frame on a 10 Mbps link that is 1,000 km long has transmission delay 20,000 / 10^7 = 2 ms and propagation delay 10^6 / (2 x 10^8) = 5 ms, so the last bit arrives 7 ms after sending begins (ignoring queuing and processing).

Line coding converts a digital bit sequence into a digital signal. NRZ-L represents 1 and 0 by two fixed voltage levels, and NRZ-I represents a 1 by inverting the level; both are bandwidth-efficient but lose synchronisation on long runs of identical bits and have a DC component. Manchester coding (used in 10 Mbps Ethernet) places a transition in the middle of every bit, a low-to-high for one value and high-to-low for the other, giving self-clocking and no DC component at the cost of twice the bandwidth; differential Manchester (Token Ring) always transitions mid-bit and encodes 0 by an extra transition at the bit start.
Going Deeper: Media Choices, Fibre Optics and Channel Limits
Guided (wired) media at a glance, from cheapest to most capable:
items: Twisted pair: two insulated copper wires twisted together; the cheapest and easiest to install, used for telephone lines and Ethernet (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a), but limited to short runs of about 100 m per Ethernet segment.

Coaxial cable: a central conductor, insulation, a braided shield and an outer jacket; better shielded and higher in bandwidth than twisted pair, used for cable TV and cable broadband and for the old 10Base2/10Base5 Ethernet; medium distances.

Optical fibre: carries light instead of electric current; the highest bandwidth and lowest attenuation, immune to electromagnetic interference, and used for Internet backbones, fibre-to-the-home and data-centre links over long distances, but the most costly to install and splice.

Correction to a common note: fibre is not 'faster' in propagation. Light in glass travels at about 2 x 10^8 m/s, roughly the speed of signals in copper; fibre's advantage is bandwidth (bits per second) and low loss, not a shorter delay, and it still suffers attenuation and dispersion even though it picks up no electrical interference.

concepts.text: Unguided (wireless) media, and where everyday systems fit:
items: Radio waves (about 3 kHz to 1 GHz in Forouzan's split): omnidirectional, long range and able to pass through walls; used for AM/FM radio, TV and paging.

Wi-Fi (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz), Bluetooth (2.4 GHz) and mobile networks are called radio systems in everyday speech; by the same split most of their carriers lie in the microwave range, but they use omnidirectional antennas and still pass through walls, with more loss at higher frequencies.
Microwaves (1 to 300 GHz) with dish or horn antennas: highly directional and need line of sight; used for point-to-point terrestrial links and satellite communication.
Infrared (300 GHz to 400 THz): very short range and blocked by walls, so neighbouring rooms do not interfere; used in TV remotes and the old IrDA links between phones and laptops.
Satellites: the lower the orbit, the shorter the delay, but the more satellites are needed to cover the Earth and the faster each one moves across the sky.

rows: Ground-satellite-ground delay (minimum: stations directly below, 3 x 10^8 m/s)

concepts.text: Light passing from a denser medium (index n1) into a less dense one (n2 < n1) bends away from the normal, following Snell's law n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2. At the critical angle the refracted ray just grazes the boundary (θ2 = 90°), and at any larger angle of incidence all the light is reflected back into the core; this is total internal reflection. The numerical aperture (NA) measures the cone of light a fibre accepts: a larger index difference gives a larger NA, which eases coupling but increases modal dispersion in multimode fibre.

concepts.plainText: Critical angle θc = arcsin(n2 / n1); numerical aperture NA = sqrt(n1^2 - n2^2), where n1 is the core index and n2 the cladding index

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: critical angle and NA of a fibre
Core n1 = 1.48, cladding n2 = 1.46
n2 / n1 = 1.46 / 1.48 = 0.98649
θc = arcsin(0.98649) = 80.6°  (rays hitting the wall above 80.6° stay in)
NA = sqrt(1.48^2 - 1.46^2) = sqrt(2.1904 - 2.1316) = sqrt(0.0588) = 0.242
Acceptance half-angle in air = arcsin(0.242) = 14.0°

Decibels turn the multiplication of gains and losses into addition: a loss of 3 dB halves the power, 10 dB divides it by 10 and 20 dB by 100. Cable loss is quoted in dB per km (about 0.2 to 0.35 dB/km for single-mode fibre, far more for copper at high frequencies), so the total loss is the rate times the length plus connector and splice losses. Absolute power is often given in dBm, decibels relative to 1 mW: 0 dBm = 1 mW, 10 dBm = 10 mW and -30 dBm = 1 µW.

Worked example 2: a power budget in dB
Transmitter power              = 10 dBm (10 mW)
5 km of cable at 3 dB/km       = -15 dB
Amplifier                      = +10 dB
Two connectors at 0.5 dB each  = -1 dB
Output = 10 - 15 + 10 - 1      = 4 dBm
In milliwatts: 10^(4/10) mW    = 2.51 mW

Worked example 3: Shannon limit first, then Nyquist levels
B = 2 MHz, SNR = 24 dB -> S/N = 10^(24/10) = 251.2
C = B log2(1 + S/N) = 2 x 10^6 x log2(252.2) = 2 x 10^6 x 7.98 = 15.96 Mbps
Choose a safer rate below the limit, e.g. 12 Mbps
Nyquist: 12 x 10^6 = 2 x 2 x 10^6 x log2 L -> log2 L = 3 -> L = 8 levels
More levels cannot push the rate above 15.96 Mbps on this channel

Worked example 4: bandwidth-delay product and bit length
Fibre link 4,000 km, v = 2 x 10^8 m/s, R = 1 Gbps
Tp  = 4 x 10^6 m / 2 x 10^8 m/s        = 20 ms
BDP = R x Tp = 10^9 x 0.02            = 2 x 10^7 bits (2.5 MB) in flight
Over a full round trip: 2 x BDP        = 4 x 10^7 bits
Length of one bit = v / R = 2 x 10^8 / 10^9 = 0.2 m
A 1,500-byte frame (12,000 bits) fills only 2.4 km of the 4,000 km

Common mistakes: convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon (S/N = 10^(dB/10)); keep bandwidth in Hz and data rate in bit/s apart; use 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s and multiply bytes by 8; do not double a one-way propagation delay unless a round trip is asked for; and remember that adding signal levels (Nyquist) helps only up to the Shannon limit, never beyond it.

formulas.plainText: SNR in dB = 10 log10(S/N); e.g. 30 dB means S/N = 1000
Transmission delay = frame length in bits / bandwidth in bits per second
Propagation delay = distance / propagation speed (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in cable)

notes.text: Convert dB to a ratio before using Shannon: S/N = 10^(dB/10). For B = 3,000 Hz and 30 dB (S/N = 1000), C = 3000 x log2(1001), about 3000 x 9.97, or roughly 30 kbps.

Nyquist gives the maximum rate for a noiseless channel with L levels, while Shannon gives the absolute capacity of a noisy channel. When both apply, Shannon is the upper limit and Nyquist tells you how many levels are needed to approach it.
Do not confuse the two delays: a faster link reduces transmission delay but not propagation delay, which depends only on distance and the medium.

formulas.title: Nyquist bit rate
formulas.plainText: C = 2B log2 L
formulas.description: Maximum bit rate of a noiseless channel of bandwidth B hertz using L discrete signal levels.

formulas.title: Shannon capacity
formulas.plainText: C = B log2(1 + S/N)
formulas.description: Theoretical maximum error-free data rate of a noisy channel, with S/N as a plain power ratio.

formulas.title: SNR in decibels
formulas.plainText: SNR_dB = 10 log10(S/N)
formulas.description: Converts a signal-to-noise power ratio to decibels; invert with S/N = 10^(dB/10).

formulas.title: Transmission delay
formulas.plainText: Tt = L / R
formulas.description: Time to place all L bits of a frame on a link of rate R bits per second.

formulas.title: Propagation delay
formulas.plainText: Tp = d / v
formulas.description: Time for a signal to travel distance d at propagation speed v through the medium.

flashcards.front: Why are the wires in twisted-pair cable twisted?
flashcards.back: Twisting makes both wires pick up nearly equal noise and crosstalk, which cancels at the receiver because it reads the difference between them.

Single-mode has an 8-10 micrometre core, one light path and a laser source for long distances; multimode has a 50/62.5 micrometre core, many paths and an LED source, limited by modal dispersion to short runs.

flashcards.front: What advantage does Manchester encoding have over NRZ?
flashcards.back: It has a transition in the middle of every bit, so it is self-clocking and has no DC component, though it needs twice the bandwidth.

questions.questionText: A channel has a bandwidth of 1 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 63. What is its Shannon capacity?
A 1,250-byte packet is sent over a 10 Mbps link that is 400 km long, with propagation speed 2 x 10^8 m/s. What is the sum of the transmission and propagation delays?
questions.explanation: Transmission delay = 10,000 bits / 10^7 bps = 1 ms; propagation delay = 4 x 10^5 m / 2 x 10^8 m/s = 2 ms; the total is 3 ms.

questions.questionText: Which multiplexing technique was designed for optical fibre and is conceptually the same as FDM, but applied to light?
questions.explanation: WDM sends several signals on different wavelengths (colours) of light through one fibre and separates them again at the receiver, exactly as FDM uses different carrier frequencies. Dense WDM carries dozens of channels on a single fibre.

questions.questionText: Which guided medium is the cheapest and most widely used for connecting desktop computers to an Ethernet LAN?
questions.explanation: UTP (Cat5e/Cat6) is cheap, flexible and easy to terminate with RJ-45 connectors, so it dominates desktop LAN connections up to 100 m. Fibre costs more and is used for backbones and long runs.

questions.questionText: What principle keeps light confined inside the core of an optical fibre?
options: Absorption of stray light by the cladding
Total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary
questions.explanation: The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so light striking the boundary at more than the critical angle is reflected completely back into the core.

questions.questionText: Which connector is used on twisted-pair Ethernet cables?
questions.explanation: Twisted-pair Ethernet uses the 8-pin RJ-45 connector. RJ-11 is the smaller telephone connector, BNC is used on coaxial cable and SC is a fibre-optic connector.

questions.questionText: Which kind of optical fibre has a very narrow core and uses a laser source, making it suitable for long-distance links?
questions.explanation: Single-mode fibre has a core of about 8-10 µm, so only one path (mode) propagates and there is no modal dispersion; with a laser source it spans tens to hundreds of kilometres.

questions.questionText: A cable made of a central copper conductor, an insulating layer, a braided metal shield and an outer plastic jacket is:
questions.explanation: That is the construction of coaxial cable; the braided outer conductor shields the centre conductor, giving better noise immunity and bandwidth than twisted pair. It is used for cable TV and cable broadband.

questions.questionText: Which wireless medium uses highly directional dish antennas that need line of sight, with relay towers spaced tens of kilometres apart?
questions.explanation: Terrestrial microwave links send a narrow beam between dish antennas, so the towers must see each other; because of the Earth's curvature, repeaters are needed roughly every 50 km.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an unguided (wireless) transmission medium?
questions.explanation: Unguided media carry electromagnetic waves through air or space with no physical conductor, as a satellite link does. Fibre, coax and twisted pair all guide the signal along a physical path.

questions.questionText: Why are the two wires in a twisted pair twisted around each other?
options: To make the cable mechanically stronger and harder to break
To increase the speed at which the signal propagates along the wire
To allow the cable to carry light pulses as well as electric current
So that noise and crosstalk affect both wires almost equally and cancel at the receiver
questions.explanation: Twisting places both wires alternately nearer to and farther from any noise source, so they pick up nearly the same interference; the receiver reads the difference between the wires, and the common noise cancels.

questions.questionText: A noiseless channel has a bandwidth of 3,000 Hz and uses binary signalling (two signal levels). What is its maximum bit rate according to the Nyquist formula?
questions.explanation: Nyquist: C = 2B log2 L = 2 x 3000 x log2 2 = 6,000 bit/s = 6 kbps. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 3 kbps.

questions.questionText: What is the minimum number of signal levels needed to send 48 kbps over a noiseless channel with a bandwidth of 4 kHz?
questions.explanation: 48,000 = 2 x 4000 x log2 L, so log2 L = 6 and L = 2^6 = 64 levels. 6 is the number of bits per level, and 4096 = 2^12 comes from forgetting the factor 2.

questions.questionText: A line with 2 MHz of usable bandwidth has a measured signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB. What is the maximum error-free data rate it can support, according to Shannon?
questions.explanation: 20 dB means S/N = 10^(20/10) = 100, so C = 2 x 10^6 x log2(101) = 2 x 10^6 x 6.66 = 13.3 Mbps. Using 20 directly as the ratio gives 8.8 Mbps.

questions.questionText: A signal loses half of its power as it travels along a cable. What is the attenuation in decibels?
questions.explanation: Attenuation = 10 log10(P2 / P1) = 10 log10(0.5) = -3.01 dB, so about -3 dB. -6 dB would be half the voltage (20 log10), and -0.3 dB forgets the factor 10.

questions.questionText: How long does it take to transmit a 1 MB file onto a 100 Mbps link, ignoring headers? Take 1 MB = 10^6 bytes and 1 Mbps = 10^6 bit/s.
questions.explanation: Transmission delay = L / R = (10^6 x 8) bits / 10^8 bit/s = 0.08 s = 80 ms. 10 ms forgets to convert bytes to bits, and 83.9 ms or 76.3 ms mix in powers of 2.

questions.questionText: What is the propagation delay over a 3,000 km optical fibre link if light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in the fibre?
questions.explanation: Propagation delay = d / v = 3 x 10^6 m / 2 x 10^8 m/s = 0.015 s = 15 ms. 10 ms wrongly uses the speed of light in vacuum, and 30 ms is the round trip.

questions.questionText: A signal passes through 4 km of cable with a loss of 3 dB/km and then through an amplifier with a gain of 7 dB. What is the overall gain of the path?
questions.explanation: Decibels add: 4 x (-3) + 7 = -12 + 7 = -5 dB, a net loss. -12 dB ignores the amplifier and -19 dB wrongly counts it as a loss.

questions.questionText: What mainly limits the distance and data rate of multimode fibre compared with single-mode fibre?
options: Modal dispersion: rays on different paths arrive at different times and spread each pulse
Electromagnetic interference picked up from power cables along the route
Crosstalk between neighbouring pairs of wires inside the cable
Its inability to carry more than one wavelength of light at a time
questions.explanation: In a wide multimode core, rays that zigzag at steep angles travel farther than axial rays, so each light pulse spreads out and adjacent pulses overlap. Fibre is immune to EMI, and crosstalk between wire pairs is a copper problem.

questions.questionText: How does graded-index multimode fibre reduce modal dispersion compared with step-index multimode fibre?
options: Its core is made of plastic, which slows every ray by the same amount so they stay together
Its thicker cladding absorbs the slower high-angle rays before they reach the receiver
Its core index is highest at the centre and falls towards the cladding, so rays on longer paths travel faster and arrive at about the same time
Its core is narrowed until only one ray can travel, exactly as in single-mode fibre
questions.explanation: Light travels faster where the refractive index is lower, so the rays that curve out towards the edge of the core make up for their longer path. This equalises arrival times far better than a step-index core.

questions.questionText: Which band of electromagnetic waves is omnidirectional, travels long distances and can pass through walls, making it suitable for AM/FM broadcasting?
questions.explanation: Radio waves (about 3 kHz to 1 GHz) spread in all directions and penetrate buildings, which suits broadcasting. Infrared and visible light are blocked by walls, and millimetre waves need line of sight.

questions.questionText: A signal goes from a ground station up to a geostationary satellite at an altitude of 35,786 km and back down to another ground station. Assuming both stations are directly below the satellite and the signal travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s, what is the propagation delay?
questions.explanation: The path is 2 x 35,786 km = 71,572 km, so the delay = 7.1572 x 10^7 / 3 x 10^8 = 0.2386 s, about 239 ms. 119 ms is the uplink only, 477 ms a full request-and-reply round trip, and 358 ms uses 2 x 10^8 m/s.

questions.questionText: Which is the lowest twisted-pair category rated to carry 10GBase-T (10 Gbps) over the full 100 m channel?
questions.explanation: Cat6a (500 MHz) supports 10GBase-T up to 100 m. Cat6 manages 10 Gbps only up to about 55 m, Cat5e (100 MHz) was designed for 1000Base-T and Cat3 for 10 Mbps.

questions.questionText: The unwanted coupling of a signal from one pair of wires into a neighbouring pair is called:
questions.explanation: Crosstalk is noise induced by the signal on an adjacent wire. Attenuation is loss of energy with distance, thermal noise comes from random electron motion, and distortion is a change of shape.

questions.questionText: A signal made of several frequency components changes shape because its components travel at different speeds and arrive at slightly different times. This impairment is called:
questions.explanation: Distortion is a change in the signal's shape caused by the different delays of its frequency components. Attenuation only reduces the strength, while impulse noise and crosstalk add unwanted energy.

questions.questionText: Which statement about optical fibre is correct?
options: Light in glass travels at about 3 x 10^8 m/s, so fibre gives a much lower propagation delay than copper
Fibre suffers no attenuation at all, so optical links never need repeaters or amplifiers
Its strengths are high bandwidth, low loss and immunity to EMI, but light in glass travels at only about 2 x 10^8 m/s
Fibre is easy to tap without being detected, which makes it less secure than copper
questions.explanation: Glass has a refractive index of about 1.5, so light in it moves at roughly 2 x 10^8 m/s, much like signals in copper. Fibre still attenuates (about 0.2-0.35 dB/km in single-mode fibre) and is hard to tap unnoticed.

questions.questionText: A channel has a bandwidth of 4 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 255. Using the Nyquist formula, how many signal levels are needed to transmit at the channel's Shannon capacity?
questions.explanation: Shannon: C = 4 x 10^6 x log2(256) = 32 Mbps. Nyquist: 32 x 10^6 = 2 x 4 x 10^6 x log2 L, so log2 L = 4 and L = 16. 256 is 1 + S/N, and 8 is log2(1 + S/N).

questions.questionText: A 1,000-byte frame is sent on a 1 Gbps link with a propagation speed of 2 x 10^8 m/s. At what link length does the propagation delay equal the transmission delay?
questions.explanation: Transmission delay = 8,000 bits / 10^9 bit/s = 8 µs. Setting d / v = 8 µs gives d = 2 x 10^8 x 8 x 10^-6 = 1,600 m = 1.6 km. 0.2 km treats bytes as bits, and 2.4 km uses 3 x 10^8 m/s.

questions.questionText: A 5,000 km fibre link runs at 1 Gbps with a propagation speed of 2 x 10^8 m/s. How many bits are in flight on the link at one time (one way), and how long is each bit on the fibre?
questions.explanation: Tp = 5 x 10^6 / 2 x 10^8 = 25 ms, so the bandwidth-delay product = 10^9 x 0.025 = 2.5 x 10^7 bits. Bit length = v / R = 2 x 10^8 / 10^9 = 0.2 m; 5 x 10^7 is the round-trip figure and 3.125 x 10^6 is the result in bytes.

questions.questionText: A transmitter launches 20 dBm into a 40 km single-mode fibre with a loss of 0.25 dB/km, and the link has two connectors with a loss of 0.5 dB each. What optical power reaches the receiver?
questions.explanation: Received power = 20 - 40 x 0.25 - 2 x 0.5 = 20 - 10 - 1 = 9 dBm, and 10^(9/10) mW = 7.94 mW. 10.0 mW ignores the connectors, 79.4 mW (19 dBm) ignores the fibre loss, and 9.00 mW reads dBm as mW.

questions.questionText: An optical fibre has a core index of 1.50 and a cladding index of 1.45. What is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary, measured from the normal?
questions.explanation: θc = arcsin(n2 / n1) = arcsin(1.45 / 1.50) = arcsin(0.9667) = 75.2°. 41.8° is the glass-to-air critical angle arcsin(1 / 1.5), and 14.8° is the complement 90° - 75.2°.

questions.questionText: A telephone channel has a bandwidth of 3 kHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 20 dB, and the modem uses 4 signal levels. What is the highest bit rate it can achieve?
questions.explanation: Nyquist with 4 levels allows 2 x 3000 x log2 4 = 12 kbps; Shannon allows 3000 x log2(1 + 100) = 19.97 kbps. The achievable rate is the smaller limit, 12 kbps; 20.0 kbps would need more levels.
